Photograph: Kim Kyung Hoon/Reuters China China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves Rob Davies Sun 6 Sep 2026 11.16 EDT Last modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 11.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth. A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly. The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth . The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn. China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry Elliott Read more The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital. The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies. The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health. “The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk. Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year. The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share ​placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco ​Corp and its subsidiaries. The two lenders said the ​proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them ​sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks ​to support growth despite weak demand for loans. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: 1:43 Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after waking from botched execution, says lawyer – video Tennessee Christa Pike ‘angry, confused’ and unable to move arms after failed execution, lawyers say Attorneys say Pike was set to be taken off life support before she woke up, as judge orders officials to preserve evidence Adam Gabbatt and Maya Yang Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.34 EDT First published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 15.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Christa Pike awoke “angry and confused” after surviving two lethal injections, her attorneys said on Wednesday, as a judge ordered Tennessee state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber last Wednesday after two supposedly lethal doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital. She was declared brain dead on Monday, her attorneys said, and her team was informed of plans to remove her from life support the next day. “But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking,” Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, said at a press conference on Wednesday. He was told her first words were “Where am I?” and “Who are you?” Pike remains hospitalized and shackled to her bed, despite pleas from medical staff for prison officials to remove her restraints, her lawyers said. She has pneumonia, a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms, they added. “There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people,” Spivey said. “She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.” Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say Read more The update on Pike’s condition came after a contentious court hearing in Nashville, where judge I’Ashea Myles ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room” during the attempted execution a week ago. Pike’s legal team accused Tennessee officials of “secreting away” evidence. Attorney Luke Ihnen said items from the attempted execution could be key to future legal challenges by Pike, should the state attempt to kill her again. “The state has made no promises that Ms Pike will not be subject to a future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes, because as we pled in January, the same thing is likely to happen,” Ihnen said. Pike, believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection, was injected withlarge doses of the sedative when Tennessee officials had attempted to put her to death, in a case that shocked many in the US and created headlines around the world. At the press conference on Wednesday, Spivey said it was unclear “what if any function” Pike would regain in her arms. “Her hands look like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” Spivey said. Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm. “Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request [by the Tennessee correction department],” he told Myles earlier. He added: “We would also amend our request and ask for that relief.” Witnesses to the attempted execution of Pike described how they heard her breathing raggedly after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her and was declared to be in critical condition. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion After the botched execution attempt, Spivey called the process “cruel and torturous” , adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered. Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins Read more Her lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward. There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination. Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995. According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her. Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years. AI (artificial intelligence) Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers Rachel Savage in Johannesburg Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.01 EDT First published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.” Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho. Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”. She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.” Kundizeza responded in a statement on X : “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work. “I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.” View image in fullscreen Journalist Vauhini Vara said she had run Kundizeza’s story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost entirely AI generated. Photograph: Andrew Altschul Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing. Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI. The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.” Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself. Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly. “I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.” Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter. Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list Read more In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.” Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software. NATO’s supreme allied commander Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, has drafted a “Theory of Victory” plan that calls for a rapid response and extensive use of drones and artificial intelligence to defeat a Russian attack. (Ronald Bell/U.S. Army) By JOHN VANDIVER STARS AND STRIPES Published October 6, 2026 · NATO is poised to unveil a new battle plan for defeating a Russian attack on its eastern flank, featuring front-line troops blunting an incursion while unleashing high-tech systems to destroy Moscow’s ability to command its forces. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s supreme allied commander and head of U.S. European Command, is expected to present the concept Monday in Warsaw, the Italian news agency Ansa reported this week . Ansa and Bloomberg obtained unclassified versions of the battle plan, which offers details on how NATO intends to fight in the event of a crisis on the alliance’s eastern edges. The concept, dubbed NATO’s Theory of Victory, lays out a sequence for responding to a potential Russian attack, such as a surprise move in the Baltic region intended to test the alliance’s commitment to collective defense. U.S. Army Col. Martin O’Donnell, a spokesperson for Grynkewich, confirmed the existence of the battle plan Tuesday without elaborating on its details. “Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” O’Donnell said. He added that NATO is a “purely defensive alliance” that does not seek conflict. Polish soldiers with the 5th Masovian Territorial Defense Brigade conduct dry-fire drills during an exercise at Bemowo Piskie Training Area, Poland, Sept. 2, 2026. (Emilie Lenglain/U.S. Army) Grynkewich will elaborate on the plans at next week’s Warsaw Security Forum, he said. For years, military commanders and security analysts have worried that Russia could attempt a land grab as a means to challenge NATO’s political willingness to act against it. Under Grynkewich’s concept, the aim would be to blunt such a move in the early stages. Forward-positioned NATO ground forces would first move to stop an incursion and then bring capabilities developed through its Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, which is focused on using drones and artificial intelligence to counter a larger opposing force, according to Ansa. The initiative has been a focal point for U.S. commanders in Europe over the past two years. Retired Gen. Christopher Donahue, who led U.S. Army Europe and Africa before relinquishing command in July , was widely seen as one of its key architects. The concept centers on adapting to a new era of warfare defined by drones, artificial intelligence and the integration of networks and data to fight more effectively. Under NATO’s Theory of Victory, such systems would help allies destroy the enemy’s command, control and targeting network through a combination of kinetic strikes and digital attacks, according to the document cited by Ansa. If necessary, NATO would then turn to more traditional heavy firepower, including combat aircraft and missiles, to destroy the enemy’s broader combat system, the news agency reported. The concept also envisions the possibility of military operations on enemy territory, according to Ansa. That suggests NATO wouldn’t limit itself to fighting Russian troops only after they crossed onto allied soil. The plan comes as military leaders and analysts debate whether Russia could exploit the time required for NATO’s political leaders to assemble a response to a sudden attack, such as a limited operation in the Baltic region. In recent years, there has been much back-and-forth debate among NATO observers about whether allies could agree fast enough to a large military response if Russia were to make a quick strike move. Under such scenarios, some experts have worried that NATO could be faced with a “fait accompli” in the Baltics, where Russia has traditionally enjoyed a force number advantage. But a former senior NATO official this week said that such a scenario overlooks how allied forces are increasingly well-positioned along the eastern flank. Retired U.S. Army Maj. Gen. Gordon “Skip” Davis Jr., a former top NATO deputy, said multinational NATO forces stationed from Finland to Romania would not have to wait for a political decision in Brussels if attacked. “Under NATO doctrine, they have the right to respond in self-defense,” Davis wrote Monday in an analysis for the Center for European Policy Analysis. “They would not need permission to respond.” NATO has multinational battlegroups across its eastern flank that are designed to be quickly reinforced under the alliance’s concepts for fighting wars. The battlegroup model was first developed in the aftermath of Russia’s initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 and has expanded in the years since. Grynkewich, as supreme allied commander, also has authority to deploy elements of NATO’s Allied Reaction Force to a threatened country without waiting for a North Atlantic Council decision, Davis said. If Russian troops crossed an allied border or launched strikes, forces already under attack could respond immediately without waiting for a collective Article 5 decision, Davis said, alluding to the key collective defense provision in the bloc’s founding document. The bigger issue facing allies in such a situation is the extent of the military response and whether to hit targets inside Russia that are enabling the attack on NATO. “You are not just going to try to catch all the arrows; you are going to strike the archer,” he said. Europe NATO John Vandiver covers U.S. military activities across Europe and Africa. Based in Stuttgart, Germany, he previously worked for newspapers in New Jersey, North Carolina and Maryland. He is a graduate of the University of Delaware.
